record.paper_title: Open problems in membrane computing and how not to solve them
record.original_question: Can every polynomial-time confluent recogniser P-system family for decision problems be simulated, with at most polynomial overhead, by a deterministic recogniser P-system family of the same sufficiently powerful model, or is there a variant of P systems in which confluent nondeterminism is strictly stronger than determinism? Here confluent means that multiple computations may occur but all computations agree on the final accepting or rejecting result, while deterministic means that the initial configuration has a single computation; the question is especially constrained by send-in communication rules that cannot distinguish among membranes with the same label and electrical charge.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider families of recogniser P systems (membrane systems) used to decide languages in polynomial time. A recogniser P system has an input membrane, halts on every computation, and outputs either "accept" or "reject". A family {Π(n)}_{n∈ℕ} of such P systems is called:

- confluent if, for every input, every computation of the corresponding P system halts and all halting computations yield the same accept/reject answer;
- deterministic if, for every input, the initial configuration admits exactly one computation.

A family decides a problem in polynomial time if the number of computation steps is bounded by a polynomial in the size of the input, and the family is uniformly constructible in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine.

Send-in communication rules are rules that move an object from the region surrounding a membrane into that membrane; such rules cannot distinguish among different membranes that share the same label and the same electrical charge.

Question. Fix a "sufficiently powerful" model of P systems (for instance, P systems with active membranes restricted so that send-in rules behave as above). Decide which of the following holds:

(a) Every confluent recogniser P system family of the model that works in polynomial time can be simulated, with at most polynomial overhead, by a deterministic recogniser P system family of the same model; or

(b) There exists a variant of P systems (within the class above) in which confluent nondeterminism is strictly more powerful than determinism, i.e., some language decidable in polynomial time by a confluent family of that variant is not decidable in polynomial time by any deterministic family of the same variant.
artifact.status_search_result: The relationship between confluence and determinism in polynomial-time recogniser P systems is a long-standing open question in membrane computing complexity. While confluent P systems are known to be simulable by deterministic Turing machines (e.g., in exponential space), no polynomial-overhead deterministic P system simulation is known, nor has a strict separation been proved for standard models. Recent work on shallow non-confluent P systems and related variants discusses the gap but does not resolve the confluent-vs-deterministic question for the polynomial-time recogniser setting.

status_evidence.title: Computational complexity in P systems
status_evidence.snippet: Each confluent basic transition P system can be efficiently simulated by a deterministic Turing machine... confluent P systems efficiently solve at most tractable problems.
status_evidence.claim: Confluent P systems are known to be simulable deterministically, but the polynomial-overhead question between confluent and deterministic recognisers within the P-system model is still discussed as open.

status_evidence.title: Shallow Non-confluent P Systems
status_evidence.snippet: Non-confluent (strongly nondeterministic) P systems with active membranes working in polynomial time are able to simulate polynomial-space nondeterministic Turing machines.
status_evidence.claim: Recent literature contrasts confluent and non-confluent power but does not settle confluence vs determinism for recogniser P-system families.
